directions: The two impugned orders dated 21st September, 2022 and 07th October, 2022, granting anticipatory bail to the respondent No. 2/accused, cannot be sustained and are quashed and set aside.
The bail bonds of the respondent No.2/accused are cancelled.

issue.issue_text: Whether the protection granted to a person under Section 438 CrPC should be limited to a fixed period so as to enable the person to surrender before the trial court and seek regular bail.

law.law_text: Section 438 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) governs the grant of anticipatory bail.
The text of Section 438 CrPC does not contain any provision that compels or obliges courts to impose a time limit on the relief granted.

When considering an application for anticipatory bail, a court should evaluate factors such as the nature of the offense, the role of the person, the likelihood of them influencing the investigation, tampering with evidence, or fleeing justice.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court held that the protection granted to a person under Section 438 CrPC should not invariably be limited to a fixed period.
It reasoned that the bail should generally continue in favour of the accused without any restriction on time.
However, the Court clarified that this is not an absolute rule. A court has the discretion to impose appropriate conditions based on the specific facts and features of a case.
This means that if the circumstances of a particular offense warrant it, a court is free to impose a condition that limits the duration of the anticipatory bail or ties it to a specific event.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC should not automatically be for a fixed period. While it can last indefinitely, courts retain the discretion to impose a time limit if the specific facts of a case justify such a condition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the life of an anticipatory bail should end at the time and stage when the accused is summoned by the court.

law.law_text: Nothing in Section 438 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) compels or obliges courts to impose conditions that limit the duration of anticipatory bail in terms of time.
The decision to grant anticipatory bail and to impose any special conditions, including time limits, is a matter of judicial discretion, dependent on the facts of the specific case.

Courts should be guided by factors such as the nature and gravity of the offense, the role of the applicant, and the likelihood of them tampering with evidence or fleeing justice when deciding on bail conditions.

application.application_text: The Court reasoned that since Section 438 CrPC does not mandate a time limit, there is no legal basis to hold that an anticipatory bail order must automatically end at a specific stage, such as when the accused is summoned or when charges are framed.
The Court determined that the protection of anticipatory bail should not be arbitrarily cut short. Instead, it held that the bail order can, and normally should, continue until the end of the trial.

While establishing this general rule, the Court preserved judicial discretion by clarifying that if a case has "special or peculiar features," the court retains the power to limit the tenure of the anticipatory bail as it sees fit.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the life or duration of an anticipatory bail order does not normally end when the accused is summoned by the court or when charges are framed. It can continue until the end of the trial, unless the court, in its discretion, decides to impose a time limit due to special or peculiar features of the case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Cooperation with an investigation is not, by itself, a sufficient ground for a court to grant or confirm an order of anticipatory bail.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's orders granting anticipatory bail were found to be clearly unsustainable because the court failed to exercise its discretion judiciously, cautiously, and in compliance with the basic principles for granting bail. Critically, the High Court also failed to recognize the prosecutrix's right to participate in the criminal proceedings by denying her a meaningful hearing on the bail application, which was a determinative factor for the Supreme Court's interference.
legal_tests_applied: The factors to be borne in mind while considering an application for bail are: (i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the offence; (ii) nature and gravity of the accusation; (iv) danger of the accused absconding or fleeing, if released on bail; (vi) likelihood of the offence being repeated; (vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being influenced; and (viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.
The right of the prosecutrix to participate in the criminal proceedings that would include a right to oppose the application for anticipatory bail moved by the accused.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant won the appeal. The following are the legal reasons the respondent's position (that bail was correctly granted) was rejected:

The High Court's order was found to be 'clearly unsustainable' as it failed to exercise its discretion 'judiciously, cautiously and strictly in compliance with the basic principles laid down in a plethora of decisions of this Court on the point.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent lost the appeal. The following are the legal reasons the appellant's position (that bail should be cancelled) succeeded:

The High Court failed to afford the appellant/prosecutrix a hearing, despite her filing an application for intervention. This denied her a meaningful hearing and amounted to a 'failure to recognize the right of the prosecutrix to participate in the criminal proceedings'.
The Court found that in a crime of this nature, where the prosecutrix is often the only witness, 'it was all the more incumbent for the High Court to have lent its ear to the appellant.'
The denial of a hearing to the prosecutrix was an 'additional factor that has prevailed with this Court to interfere in the impugned orders.'
policy_considerations: The right of a prosecutrix to participate in criminal proceedings, which includes the right to oppose an anticipatory bail application, cannot be whittled down merely because the State is represented in the proceedings.
In crimes where there is ordinarily no other witness except for the prosecutrix herself, it is particularly incumbent upon the court to provide her with a hearing.

While deciding a bail application, courts ought to refrain from undertaking a detailed analysis of the evidence to prevent any prejudice to the case of either the prosecution or the defence before the trial is concluded.
